Tom Hiddleston says happiness is overrated and spending your life chasing it can actually make you unhappy

"Meaning is a structure that only you create in your own life, an architecture with your own particular spiritual fingerprint, whereby if you're going through a hard time, if you're going through challenge, struggle, obstacles, suffering or pain, only you know why you're going through it"

"You might know, this is hard now. I'm doing it for my kids. I'm doing it for my mom. I'm doing it for my future"

candidates.text:
POLYMARKET: DEM SWEEP?

I don’t trust polling data. 

But, I have a lot more confidence in market based mechanisms like Polymarket & Kalshi.  

Back in 2024, I had a non-consensus view that Trump would win. 

That contrarian view was based on:
- the composition of early voting turn out
- new voter registrations
- prediction markets.

Here’s how those indicators look today:

1) We don’t see that same early voting composition effect this year. 

2) The Rs did gain on newly Registered Voters in swing states. 

That’s a win in the R camp…

BUT, the last six months have likely washed away that edge as turnout shows differently. 

3) In 2024, Trump won on bread and butter issues like inflation (and immigration control). 

4) The inflation story and high gas prices - keeps this as a ‘kitchen table issue’. 

The social media signals show high levels of dissatisfaction (really with both parties). 

5) Trump’s base of influencers like Tucker Carlson, Candace Owens, etc are not supporting this time. 

So, those voters are less likely to turn out. 

But, then where is the new marginal voter for Trump?

6) S&P futures are down (somewhat) after the close 

Big picture: Post Mid-Years are quite bullish since 1950 as uncertainty recedes. 

Stock prices follow earnings, and valuations have reset.

.@dylan522p says a common misconception is that most AI spend in the hard sciences is going toward discovery, when in reality the vast majority is going to engineering. 

He explains why that's a good thing:

"You have to get really good at the engineering before you can discover something and bring it to market."

"It's not about inventing a new material. In semiconductors, if you improve the deposition of something, and so then your chip has less resistance, or you can shrink it a bit further, that's so much economic value that is *immediately* delivered."

"Chips sit on substrates. Substrates route the wires in and out, and power in. The substrates for CPUs — the yields there are in the range of 40 to 60%. What if those yields become 95%? The economic value that's generated is massive."

"Or take an Intel fab. Its fab yields are lower than TSMC. If its yields are all of a sudden higher than TSMC, or equivalent, the economic value that can be delivered is massive."

candidates.text:
This is the kind of tech "storytelling" that is loved by a dense echochamber of people who constantly seek each other's validation of being close to the technology frontier, but means nothing to the common person. "Force" is common to such storytelling -- it'll use examples from history, from the renaissance, from a successful person's speech, from everything in the past that had little to do with the way technology exists today to make the stale point that today is so much better. And in doing so, it will coldly defy plain logic, allowing gaping fallacies to creep in because the echo chambers will anyway never object because being "pilled" is their entire identity, common sense be damned. 

One could ask, even for this lousy piece of writing, does it really make sense to compare such accomplished people from history who lived memorable and fulfilling lives and went on to do great and memorable things that will outlive them forever with... the modern man waking up on a cushy mattress in an air conditioned room where he/she turns on the laptop to be glued to a screen for the rest of their day, and then to imply that the latter has it better than the former who are dead (without whom the modern man seemingly cannot even describe his thoughts)? 

What of the air outside this modern joe's home, the air that chokes him and his children, made not better but worse by the same technologies this piece of writing describes as a "dance on the grave of dead problems that dead people thought could never die"?

"Dead problems" -- have we lost our eyes, or our minds? DEAD PROBLEMS? Step outside, will you?

It is a pity that those of us who owe technology much of our career and sense of purpose and love it in ways that are not quite as blind must be made to constantly wrestle with our relationship with it, because the echo chambers would have us believe that if we don't share in such foolish and nauseating levels of technology worship then we don't belong here.

I say bullshit. 

I refuse to be blind, I refuse to be "pilled". I am not going to pretend that an air conditioner is a compensation for that which technology does horribly against the world, let alone symbolic of us dancing on the graves of the forefathers and foremothers of humanity far greater than us. And that does not end my relationship with technology, but instead nourishes it.
